title: Nothing on any make is documented as a liquid-cooled battery — what each maker's documents call air-cooled, liquid-cooled or leave unstated
description: Generic-layer entry for the cooling architecture, written as what cools the pack, the motor, the controller and the charger on each make and how each make's own documents describe it; this entry also corrects the premise of roadmap row 249, 'liquid cooling loops (battery)'. No manufacturer document read describes a liquid-cooled battery on any of the three makes. Zero's manuals describe no coolant at all and call the powertrain "passively air-cooled". Energica's Eva manual says only that the central battery compartment "allows cooling of the battery", and its technology page credits "specific ventilation paths". LiveWire's service manuals route coolant through the on-board charger, the controller electronics and the motor, and none of their coolant-flow descriptions or hose procedures includes the RESS, although two S2 steps name a "battery charger to RESS coolant hose". No LiveWire document states how the RESS is cooled. Zero: neither the 2025 owner's manual for the S, SR, SR/F and SR/S (part 8811984-AF) nor the 2021 SR/F owner's manual (part 88-09445-01), both read from dealer-hosted mirror copies, mentions coolant, a radiator, a pump or a fan; section 4.11 of the 2025 manual says "this passively air-cooled powertrain cannot be operated indefinitely at high power/high rpm without reaching its thermal limitations", and the specification tables' Controller and power-pack Type rows state no cooling method (section 8.18); the motor's own air-cooled Type line is in the Zero platform entry. On the 2014-2021 S, SR, DS and DSR (the platform this corpus calls Cypher II), Zero's 2020 service manual (Version 1, archived dealer copy) bolts the Sevcon controller to a separate heat sink ('HEATSINK #4 CONTROLLER SDS', 'R CONTROLLER HEATSINK'), and the heat sink bolts to the frame; on the 2025 street models the controller sits on a 'controller carrier' bolted to the power pack (2025 owner's manual section 6.6), and its part description is in the Zero controller-recall entry. Energica (the Energica Eva owner's manual, Cod. ENF003100 Rev. 02 (February 2018), which names the Eva 80 and Eva 107 and whose sample labels read model year 2016 (read from a mirror copy)): the central battery compartment "allows cooling of the battery" and must be kept clear of "leaves, pebbles, paper or any foreign body" (printed page 121); the only coolant in the Liquids table is the inverter's (printed page 72, named in the Energica motor entry); the only fan the manual names is the on-board charger's, "the battery charger cooling fan situated in the compartment under the seat must be kept clear of any objects which could obstruct the air flow" (printed page 57); the manual never describes the cooling circuit, with no radiator, thermostat, expansion tank or diagram, although its code table lists a water pump and motor and drive coolant sensors and it calls the motor oil-cooled. Energica's technology web page (archived captures of June 19, 2019 and July 9, 2021) says the pack's cooling uses "specific ventilation paths that limit the stress of the batteries", naming no medium or fan; the archived Experia page (capture of March 29, 2023) gives the motor as "Liquid-Cooled 3-Phase with Adaptive Control Inverter", the current Experia page drops those words, and the current Ego, Eva Ribelle and EsseEsse9 pages name a cooling method only on the motor line, not in their Battery & Charging block. LiveWire: the 2021 LiveWire ONE service manual (94000865, Harley-Davidson's Service Information Portal) gives the coolant flow as "Radiator (3) to onboard charger (1)", "Onboard charger (1) to coolant pump (7)", "Coolant pump (7) to inlet fitting (6)", through the VSC and MCM inside the electric vehicle powertrain, and "Outlet fitting (4) to radiator (3)"; the 2024 S2 service manual (94001237) runs it from the radiator to the power electronics unit, which "contains the Onboard Charger (OBC) and Vehicle Supervisory Controller (VSC)", to a pump in the bottom of the motor housing, "into the motor housing (5), through a network of passages", back through a return channel in the power electronics unit and into the radiator. Both service manuals give the inverter as "Integrated Gate Bipolar Transistor (IGBT), water cooled", where the owner's manuals say only 'IGBT'. The ONE's six and the S2's seven coolant-hose procedures name no RESS hose; the ONE's RESS removal carries the note "Do not disconnect coolant lines." on the charger step, unclips the coolant hoses from the front of the RESS (step 41) and swings the "battery charger, steering head and cooling system assembly" away intact (step 47). The S2 service manual's power-electronics Prepare and Complete steps (step 8 of each) name a "battery charger to RESS coolant hose" that its coolant flow, hose procedures and RESS removal do not show; the contradiction is unresolved in the manual. The S2 radiator carries electric cooling fans ("Cooling Fan Assembly", connector "Cooling fan [234]"); the ONE service manual has no fan, and neither manual publishes fan logic. How it shows: on a Zero there is no coolant to service and heat leaves through the powertrain's own surfaces; on an Energica the manual asks for the battery compartment and the charger fan to be kept clear; on a LiveWire the coolant loop serves the charger, the controller electronics and the motor. The LiveWire emergency-response guides and the 2020 parts catalogue could not be read, so whether a RESS coolant fitting exists as a part is not established. The Energica manual statements are anchored to the Eva owner's manual ENF003100 Rev. 02 only; no owner's or service manual for the EMCE bikes or the Experia is published.
model: Zero S, SR, SR/F, SR/S, DS, DSR (2021 and 2025 owner's manuals; 2020 service manual); Energica Eva (owner's manual ENF003100 Rev. 02), Ego, Eva Ribelle, EsseEsse9, Experia; Harley-Davidson LiveWire (ELW, 2020), LiveWire ONE (LW1) and LiveWire S2 Del Mar, Alpinista, Mulholland
symptoms: does an electric motorcycle have coolant
what does the coolant loop cool
air cooled or liquid cooled motor
causes: Assuming a liquid-cooled battery, which no maker in this corpus documents
Looking for a coolant circuit on a Zero, which has none
Blocking the battery compartment or charger fan airflow on an Energica
fix_procedure: 1. Identify what the make cools with what before diagnosing a heat complaint: Zero, nothing liquid; Energica, a battery compartment the manual says allows cooling of the battery, a fan-cooled charger and a coolant circuit the manual does not map; LiveWire, a coolant loop through the charger, the controller electronics and the motor. 2. Do not tell an owner whether the battery is cooled by liquid or by air; no document read says either for certain. 3. On an Energica, keep the central battery compartment and the under-seat charger fan clear. 4. On a LiveWire S2, the radiator fans have no published control logic; a fan that never runs is a dealer diagnosis. 5. On a Cypher II Zero, the controller's heat path is its heat sink; see the cooling-faults entry for its service.

title: Motor and controller temperature on each make — a gauge with no number behind the red, a thermal strategy with no curve, and no motor gauge at all on some
description: Generic-layer entry for motor and controller temperature and the powertrain's thermal strategy, written as what each make does when the motor or controller gets hot and how each make shows it, anchored to the manufacturer's own document for every make named. No maker publishes a derating curve, percentage, trigger temperature or time limit for motor or controller power; the documents give only ratings, which carry no temperature. The battery's own temperature limits are in the battery thermal-derating entry, and the motor and controller temperature codes are in the motor-controller fault entry. Zero: the 2025 owner's manual (8811984-AF, section 4.12, mirror copy) and the 2021 SR/F owner's manual (88-09445-01, section 4.12) give the motor temperature gauge as White 68°F (20°C) to 244°F (118°C) and Red 244°F (118°C) to 302°F (150°C), and say "The battery and motor temperature gauges do not have a numerical value display function"; neither says what happens at 118 °C or whether red matches the thermal strategy or a temperature code. The 2025 quadrant-gauge table (section 3.27) nevertheless offers "Motor Temp" in "Degrees (°F or °C)" (the 2021 SR/F: 'Motor Temperature', quadrant A or B only), while the dash illustrations show a thermometer icon with no number; the manual does not reconcile the two. The thermal strategy: at sustained high speed "your motorcycle will be gradually slowed down to the point that the top speed of the bike is "sustainable," from a thermal standpoint", and in another sustained high-power event, such as continued powering through a low traction surface, power will simply be reduced; no rate, percentage, duration or trigger temperature is given (section 4.11 in both manuals). Section 3.24, row G, says performance is reduced "until the component has cooled sufficiently", with no key cycle, time or reset. Section 2.2 warns "Using partial throttle for hill-holding will heat up the motor and potentially limit peak power and torque until the motor cools." The only proxies for derating are ratings: the 2025 SR/F (Europe) table gives 83 kW peak against 34 kW "Maximum Continuous-rated 30 Minutes Power (According to UNECE Regulation No. 85)", and 200 km/h maximum against 170 km/h sustained (section 8.18); the rest-of-world tables have no R85 row. On the 2014-2021 S, SR, DS and DSR (the corpus's Cypher II), the 2021 owner's manual (88-09447-01) says "The yellow temperature indicator light (A) on the lower dash has two informational stages": flashing means powertrain components "are approaching their temperature limit. Performance will not be affected", and slowing until it stops flashing avoids "an enforced power reduction"; solid means the limit is exceeded and "Performance will be reduced until the component(s) have cooled sufficiently" (sections 4.5 and 3.11); the later manuals describe a red light, solid only. Its dash codes 2 and 3 'Motor Temperature Warning Stage 1' and 'Stage 2' and 22 'Board Temperature Error' carry descriptions only, with no thresholds. The same numbers mean different things by platform: on the 2021 S, SR, DS and DSR, 41 is 'Low Battery Voltage Disable', 55 'Internal Fault Error', 56 'Monolith Not Connected' and 57 'Module Did Not Connect'; on the 2021 SR/F and 2025 models, 41 is 'Motor High Temperature' and 57 'Controller High Temperature', with 55 and 56 the battery temperature codes; identify the platform before reading a code (see the Zero platform entry). Display B's 'Temp' field is the motor's temperature per the 2021 owner's manual and 'the motor, battery, and controller' per the 2020 service manual, and both say it may not read accurately during the first 5 miles of a ride. Zero's firmware release notes page (a manufacturer web page, 'Updated: August 12, 2026') carries no motor or controller thermal, limit or derating item. Energica (the Energica Eva owner's manual, Cod. ENF003100 Rev. 02 (February 2018), which names the Eva 80 and Eva 107 and whose sample labels read model year 2016 (read from a mirror copy)): the dash shows no motor or drive temperature; its only temperatures are 'Air temperature' and 'Battery temperature' in the display overview (printed page 33), and none of the lamps in the dashboard key is a temperature or coolant lamp (printed page 27); motor and drive heat reach the rider through the amber LIMP lamp, the LIMP messages and the codes in the motor-controller fault entry. The repair-information sheet ('COMPONENT AND DIAGNOSIS INFORMATION', Rev. 15/05/2018, mirror copy) lists OBD PID 05 'Engine coolant temperature' without saying which sensor feeds it, and whether a generic scan tool returns it is untested. 'Nominal continuous power' per EU regulation 168/2013 (Eva 80: 80 kW; Eva 107: 107 kW) is a rating with no duration or temperature (printed page 63), and the current Ego web page gives 'Peak 169 hp (126 kW) (EMCE)' and 'Sustained 147 hp (110 kW) (EMCE)'. LiveWire: no owner's manual of the 2020 LiveWire (94000703), the LiveWire ONE (94001019) or the S2 (94001315) publishes a derating curve, percentage, threshold or time limit for motor or inverter power, and no alert in their alert tables names motor or inverter over-temperature; the Propulsion Limited indicator and the Temp widget are in the motor-controller fault entry. How it shows: a hot motor or controller on a Zero lights the temperature indicator and slows the bike to a sustainable speed; on an Energica it shows only as LIMP; on a LiveWire no owner-facing alert names it. The Energica manual statements are anchored to the Eva owner's manual ENF003100 Rev. 02 only; no owner's or service manual for the EMCE bikes or the Experia is published.
model: Zero S, SR, SR/F, SR/S, DS, DSR (2021 and 2025 owner's manuals; 2020 service manual); Energica Eva (owner's manual ENF003100 Rev. 02), Ego, Eva Ribelle, EsseEsse9, Experia; Harley-Davidson LiveWire (ELW, 2020), LiveWire ONE (LW1) and LiveWire S2 Del Mar, Alpinista, Mulholland
symptoms: motor temperature gauge in the red
bike slows down at high speed
power drops on a long climb
motor gets hot holding on a hill
no motor temperature on the dash
causes: Sustained high speed or high power pushing the powertrain to its thermal limit (Zero thermal strategy)
Hill-holding on partial throttle heating the motor (Zero)
Reading a Zero code number without the platform, where 41, 55, 56 and 57 mean different things
fix_procedure: 1. On a Zero, read the temperature indicator and the motor gauge: a flashing yellow light on the 2014-2021 models is a warning with no power loss, a solid light means power is reduced until the powertrain cools; slow down and let it cool. 2. Identify the Zero platform before reading codes 41, 55, 56 or 57. 3. Do not hill-hold on the throttle; use the brakes. 4. On an Energica, a heat problem shows only as LIMP and its codes; see the motor-controller fault entry. 5. On a LiveWire, no owner-facing alert names motor heat; a power limit with no other cause is a dealer diagnosis. 6. Do not quote a derating curve or trigger temperature; none is published.

title: The cooling loop's own faults and service on each make — pump and fan codes, a coolant lamp whose number is only in the service manual, and Zero with no loop at all
description: Generic-layer entry for the cooling system's own faults and service, written as what fails in the cooling hardware and how each make shows it, anchored to the manufacturer's own document for every make named; the battery's temperature faults are in the battery thermal-derating entry and the controller's temperature codes in the motor-controller fault entry. Zero: there is no coolant loop to fault. The 2025 owner's manual's 17-item maintenance schedule (8811984-AF, sections 6.2 to 6.5, mirror copy) has no motor-fin, heat-sink or cooling item, its only drive-motor item being 'Drive Motor – Commissioning and timing', and section 6.39 names the power pack and controller only in "Avoid spraying water of great force around the dash unit, charge port, power pack, and controller." On the 2014-2021 S, SR, DS and DSR (the corpus's Cypher II), Zero's 2020 service manual (Version 1, archived dealer copy) requires thermal grease between controller and heat sink, "A layer of thermal grease (such as Dow Corning® 340) MUST be applied as described below, before bolting the brushless motor controller to the heat sink", warns that "too little thermal compound will not fill all gaps of the contact surfaces, but too much thermal compound may prevent the gap from closing up when tightening", starts by cleaning old grease from the controller face, and gives the heat-sink bolts as 7 N·m (5 lb ft) for the size 4 controller and 11 N·m (8 lb ft) for size 6 and the heat sink to the frame as 26 N·m (19 lb ft), where the 2021 owner's manual (88-09447-01, section 6.6) gives the rear heat-sink bolt as 24 Nm (18 lb·ft), a difference between two documents of different model years. The same service manual lists motor and controller temperature warning codes 2 to 5 with descriptions only and gives no procedure for them. Energica (the Energica Eva owner's manual, Cod. ENF003100 Rev. 02 (February 2018), which names the Eva 80 and Eva 107 and whose sample labels read model year 2016 (read from a mirror copy)): the code table lists water-pump codes P0A07 WATER PUMP OPEN CIRCUIT FAULT, P0A06 WATER PUMP SHORT CIRCUIT FAULT and P0A05 WATER PUMP LOCKED (printed pages 79 and 80), charger-fan codes P1040 CHARGER FAN OPEN CIRCUIT FAULT, P1041 CHARGER FAN SHORT CIRCUIT FAULT and P1042 CHARGER FAN LOCKED (printed page 79), and charger temperature shutdown codes P1037 CHARGER HIGH TEMPERATURE SHUTDOWN (PRIMARY OR SECONDARY) and P1038 CHARGER LOW TEMPERATURE SHUTDOWN with a PSU over-temperature code P0A08 PSU OVER MAXIMUM TEMPERATURE (printed page 78); none lights the MIL, none has a message, a LIMP link, a temperature value or a remedy, the manual does not say what the pump serves, and it never defines 'PSU'. The coolant level check removes the left lateral cover, the left upper lateral fairing (disconnecting the front left turn signal) and the tank cover, and reads the reservoir label between its min and max marks with the motorcycle perfectly vertical; "The coolant may become very hot (up to 80°C / 176°F). To avoid possible burns, top up only when the coolant is at low temperature." (printed pages 114 to 116). The schedule's 'Cooling system — check the level and for leaks. Top up if necessary' row is the only cooling row: there is no radiator, fan, coolant-hose, pump or thermostat item (printed page 108; the coolant replacement interval is in the Energica service entry). LiveWire: the owner's manuals' Coolant temperature indicator "illuminates when the coolant has exceeded threshold temperature", and if the level is sufficient and it stays on, see a dealer; no power reduction is described (2020 LiveWire owner's manual 94000703, printed page 89; the LiveWire ONE and S2 manuals say the same). The number behind it is only in the service manuals: 'Coolant system temperature lamp' 178 °F (81 °C) (2021 LiveWire ONE service manual 94000865, Cooling System General, Table 3; the 2024 S2 service manual 94001237 is identical), with the pressure cap's lower limit 18 psi (124 kPa), rated 20 psi (138 kPa) and upper limit 22 psi (152 kPa) in Table 2, and a Pressure Cap Test that replaces a cap venting below 124 kPa (18.0 psi) or above 152 kPa (22.0 psi). The ONE service manual's pump table has the body control module switch the pump on a request from the VSC or the on-board charger, On for AC charging, a high DC-to-DC temperature, propulsion enabled and vehicle upright, and Off for a tipped vehicle, a critical pump fault, a faulted body control module or charger, or an open circuit to the pump; "Pump will run after vehicle shutdown until 80 °C (176 °F) is reached or one minute, whichever occurs first", without saying which temperature is read. The service manuals' High Temperature causes add "Faulty coolant pump" and "Air in system" to the owner's-manual list in the LiveWire thermostat entry, and list Coolant Leaks causes. Alerts: the 2020 manual's Table 37 has 'Alert – OBC Over Temperature / OBC overheating / Shutdown motorcycle and allow to cool' and 'Alert – Coolant Pump Fault / Coolant pump fault. / See dealer'; the LiveWire ONE keeps the pump alert, keeps OBC Over Temperature for the rectangle instrument, and adds for the round instrument 'OBC Too Warm / OBC general fault / See dealer' and 'RESS Too Warm / RESS general fault / See dealer'; the S2 alert table has no coolant-pump, charger-temperature or motor-temperature row. While charging, 'Onboard Charger (OBC) TOO WARM / OBC above operating temperature.' carries the action 'Verify unobstructed airflow to radiator. Restart charge after vehicle cools down.' (S2; the ONE's charging widget has the same charger row). No NHTSA recall for any of the three makes concerns motor, controller or coolant-loop cooling. Zero's campaigns with a temperature or fire consequence are pack campaigns: 13V257 (2013 FX and XU), whose consequence reads 'possibly resulting in a rapid temperature increase and off-gassing of the cells' electrolyte which may cause a burn to the rider' and which is the campaign in the Zero battery-campaign entry, and 18V215, 'An electrical short can increase the risk of a fire'; 14V119, filed under 'ENGINE AND ENGINE COOLING', is a rotor-to-stator motor campaign. LiveWire's four campaigns (20V624, 24V149, 24V216, 24V601) are software, fastener and fuse campaigns, and NHTSA lists no Energica recall. The Energica manual statements are anchored to the Eva owner's manual ENF003100 Rev. 02 only; no owner's or service manual for the EMCE bikes or the Experia is published.
model: Zero S, SR, SR/F, SR/S, DS, DSR (2021 and 2025 owner's manuals; 2020 service manual); Energica Eva (owner's manual ENF003100 Rev. 02), Ego, Eva Ribelle, EsseEsse9, Experia; Harley-Davidson LiveWire (ELW, 2020), LiveWire ONE (LW1) and LiveWire S2 Del Mar, Alpinista, Mulholland
causes: Low coolant, air in the loop, a failed pump or a blocked radiator on a LiveWire
An obstructed radiator or charger airflow while charging (LiveWire, Energica)
A water-pump or charger-fan circuit fault (Energica codes)
Missing or wrong thermal grease between a Cypher II Zero controller and its heat sink
fix_procedure: 1. LiveWire: with the coolant temperature lamp on, check the level cold; if it is sufficient and the lamp stays on, it is dealer work. The lamp's number, 178 °F (81 °C), is in the service manual. Check the cap against its test limits, look for air in the system and for a failed pump, and keep the radiator airflow clear, especially while charging. 2. Energica: read the pump, fan and charger-temperature codes; none lights the MIL, so check the diagnostics screen. Check the coolant level cold, bike vertical, between the marks. Keep the charger fan's airflow clear. 3. Zero: there is no coolant; on a Cypher II controller replacement, apply the thermal grease as the service manual directs before torquing the heat sink. 4. No recall concerns cooling on any of the three makes; do not look for one.

title: Ambient heat and cold on each make — what the manuals say about riding, parking and storing, apart from the battery's own limits
description: Generic-layer entry for ambient temperature and riding, written as what each make says about heat and cold outside the battery's own limits and how each make shows the air temperature, anchored to the manufacturer's own document for every make named; the battery's temperature limits, the cold-weather range figure, the storage temperature ranges and the charging windows are in the battery thermal-derating and cycle-count entries, and the cold-pack regen limit in the regen limits entry. No manual ties the air temperature to motor or controller power reduction. Zero: the 2025 owner's manual (8811984-AF, section 7.8, mirror copy) says cold-weather operation "has no permanent impact on its power pack/cells", and that "In extreme cold weather the motorcycle may also experience a temporary reduction in power and, correspondingly, achieved top speed"; the same text is in the 2021 SR/F, 2021 S/SR/DS/DSR and 2020 service manuals. Its cold-riding recommendation (in the thermal-derating entry) is set on the power pack's temperature, not the air's, and a pack ridden below it "needs to be put on the charger", inside that entry's charging window, "as soon as the ride is concluded". In heat, "Operation of the motorcycle in hot temperatures should not result in any noticeable performance changes" (section 7.9), its one riding limit being the pack cut-off in the thermal-derating entry, and no Zero manual ties the air temperature to the thermal strategy of section 4.11. To protect the pack, Zero says to avoid leaving the motorcycle parked in direct sunlight (section 6.9, item 2), and adds: "Storing the motorcycle or its power pack in direct sunlight in ambient temperatures above 105°F (41°C) may result in accelerated permanent decay of power pack performance, and hence it is not recommended" (section 7.9 note; 2021 SR/F section 7.8). The 2025 quadrant-gauge table offers an 'Ambient Temp' gauge in 'Degrees (°F or °C)' (section 3.27). While the 12 V battery warms (the cold-start lockout in the thermal-derating entry), the dash shows '12V Battery Heating up', the motorcycle is released once the 12 V battery "is determined to be above 32°F (0°C)", and codes 22 '12V Battery Heater Short Fault' and 23 '12V Battery Heater Disconnect Fault' are the heater's own faults (section 7.8; notification and codes in chapter 7). Energica (the Energica Eva owner's manual, Cod. ENF003100 Rev. 02 (February 2018), which names the Eva 80 and Eva 107 and whose sample labels read model year 2016 (read from a mirror copy)): the dash shows 'Air temperature' in °C or °F, and 'The "Warning: ice" symbol is displayed at temperatures below 4°C (39.2°F)' (printed page 34); 'temperature' is one of the range factors in which "even small changes may produce significant differences", with no figure, and ECO mode "automatically controls all factors concerning power consumption (motor power, heating etc.)" without explaining the heating (printed page 37); for a long lay-up the manual gives no storage temperature and says to "Store the motorcycle in a dry place away from sudden temperature changes" under a tarpaulin that will not "retain condensation" (printed page 121), with no guidance on sun or heat. The repair-information sheet (Rev. 15/05/2018) lists OBD PID 46 'Ambient air temperature'. LiveWire: no owner's manual of the 2020 LiveWire (94000703), the LiveWire ONE (94001019) or the S2 (94001315) gives a riding or storage temperature range for the motorcycle itself; the only ranges printed in the S2 manual are the portable charger's, 'Only operate the portable charger in temperatures within its operating range of -20–50 °C (-4–122 °F), and with the control box out of direct sunlight', and a storage range of -40–80 °C (-40–176 °F). Extended storage at excessive hot or cold ambient temperature is a RESS warranty exclusion, with its figures in the cycle-count entry. For cold climates the service manuals' Freeze Point Test says to "Compare the freeze point of the coolant to the anticipated operating or storage temperatures. Replace as required", using coolant tester HD-26568 (°C) or HD-23688 (°F), and where the expected cold exceeds the premix's protection (given in the LiveWire thermostat entry) to replace the coolant with de-ionized water and ethylene glycol mixed to a lower freeze point; the same manual's Drain and Fill notice says "Use of other coolants/mixtures may lead to motorcycle damage" (2021 LiveWire ONE service manual 94000865; the 2024 S2 service manual is identical). How it shows: cold shows as range and, in extreme cold, power; heat shows on a Zero only through the pack cut-off and on the others not at all in the owner's documents; the air temperature is on the dash of the Zero 2025 and the Energica. The Energica manual statements are anchored to the Eva owner's manual ENF003100 Rev. 02 only; no owner's or service manual for the EMCE bikes or the Experia is published.
model: Zero S, SR, SR/F, SR/S, DS, DSR (2021 and 2025 owner's manuals; 2020 service manual); Energica Eva (owner's manual ENF003100 Rev. 02), Ego, Eva Ribelle, EsseEsse9, Experia; Harley-Davidson LiveWire (ELW, 2020), LiveWire ONE (LW1) and LiveWire S2 Del Mar, Alpinista, Mulholland
symptoms: riding an electric motorcycle in winter
storing the bike in a hot garage
causes: Extreme cold temporarily reducing power and top speed (Zero)
Parking or storing in direct sun or heat, which the makers say ages the pack
A coolant mixture whose freeze point is above the expected cold (LiveWire)
The 12 V battery warm-up holding the bike after a cold soak (Zero)
fix_procedure: 1. In cold weather expect less range and, in extreme cold, less power on a Zero; the pack is not harmed. After a ride on a cold pack, put it on the charger as Zero directs. 2. A Zero held at start-up in the cold is warming its 12 V battery; wait for the release. Codes 22 and 23 are the heater's own faults. 3. Park in shade: Zero warns against direct sun, and against storing in direct sun above the temperature its manual gives. 4. Energica: store dry, away from sudden temperature changes, under a cover that does not trap condensation; the ice symbol is an air-temperature warning, not a fault. 5. LiveWire: in a cold climate, test the coolant's freeze point against the expected cold and use the manual's replacement rule, keeping to the coolant it specifies.
